scenario: AITA for wanting my girlfriend to be less braggy about her work perks? She seems to forget that the way she lives isn't how most people live... | My girlfriend has a pretty sweet job. She doesn't have set hours; she just has to work 35 hours a week whenever is convenient for her and make it to her few meetings. She can work from the office or from home sometimes. She has a full benefits package despite being under what most people consider full time. A really nice retirement package too. And the company will pay everything for continued education. She does work she finds interesting (cutting edge robotics) and gets along well with her coworkers. She has a lot of PTO per year and her boss even lets the employees "earn up" more; if they work extra hours one week they can ask for the equivalent in PTO for later. Her team's managers buy them whatever they want for the office; they want a 500 dollar expresso maker, they get it. They want a type of fancy coffee, they get it. Nice furniture, done... They get paid well too; pretty middle of the road salary for robotics but she says the work life balance more than makes up for it. She'd rather have more time than be a top earner. And honestly a midrange robotics salary is still damn good. And anyway, For a while I thought "good for her" for having found something that she is happy with. But recently it's gotten frustrating because I think she forgets that this isn't how everyone lives. Like when we're out with my friends or just hanging out she'll talk about the nice stuff her managers bought for the office, about all the vacations she takes, about how she and her coworkers left the office in the middle of the day to see a movie then came back and just worked a little later. And yeah, it seems like she forgets that is no way a normal job. So last night we were at a party and she mentioned how she was going to tour a few new apartments Monday morning and afternoon, and one of the people at the party was like "don't you have work" and she said "yeah but I can set my own hours" And that just rubbed me the wrong way and I said that she needed to stop going on and on about her work perks, it was obnoxious and came off braggy. She was like "I was just explaining something" and I said it wasn't just this, it was everything. Most people don't live the life she lives." She said that I was coming off jealous and that it was a bad look. That she was where she was because she didn't settle for less; she studied and worked her ass off, and didn't let herself get too settled anywhere she was unfulfilled. And that instead of complaining, maybe I should ask myself what I'm feeling jealous of and what I need to do to get it. I told her she was missing the point; she'll always be around people who don't have what she does, and she could be a little more modest about it. She said I was the only one who seemed to have a problem with it, and stormed off... AITA for what I said?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm being AITA (A Guy In The Arena) for wanting my girlfriend to be less braggy about her work perks. Let me break this down step by step. First, I need to understand what AITA means. From what I know, AITA is a term used in online communities where someone is questioning whether they're being too harsh or unreasonable in a situation, often involving relationships or social interactions. So, in this case, I'm wondering if I'm being too hard on my girlfriend for talking about her job benefits. Now, looking at the situation: My girlfriend has a pretty sweet job. She doesn't have set hours, just needs to work 35 hours a week whenever it's convenient. She can work from home sometimes, has full benefits, a nice retirement package, and the company pays for continued education. She works in cutting-edge robotics, gets along with her coworkers, has a lot of PTO, and her boss even lets them "earn up" more time off. Her team's managers buy them nice office stuff, like a $500 espresso maker and fancy coffee, and they have nice furniture. They're paid well too, with a mid-range salary for robotics, but the work-life balance makes it worth it. She prefers more time over being a top earner. Initially, I thought it was great that she found something she's happy with. But lately, it's been frustrating because I feel she forgets that not everyone lives like that. When we're out with friends or just hanging out, she talks about the nice stuff her managers bought, all the vacations she takes, how she and her coworkers left the office in the middle of the day to see a movie and came back later. It seems like she doesn't realize this isn't normal. Last night at a party, she mentioned she was going to tour some new apartments Monday morning and afternoon. Someone asked, "Don't you have work?" and she replied, "Yeah, but I can set my own hours." That rubbed me the wrong way, and I told her she needed to stop going on and on about her work perks because it was obnoxious and came off as braggy. She said she was just explaining something, but I said it wasn't just this one thingâĢĶit was everything. Most people don't live the life she does. She responded by saying I was coming off as jealous and that it was a bad look. She said she's where she is because she didn't settle for less; she studied and worked hard, didn't let herself get too settled where she was unfulfilled. Instead of complaining, I should ask myself what I'm feeling jealous of and what I need to do to get it. I told her she was missing the point; she'll always be around people who don't have what she does, and she could be a little more modest about it. She said I was the only one with a problem and stormed off. So, am I being AITA for what I said? Let me think about this. On one hand, I can see why I'm frustrated. It's easy to feel like she's bragging, especially when she's talking about things that most people don't have. It can come off as if she's flaunting her lifestyle, which might make others feel inferior or envious. I don't like feeling jealous, and it's understandable that I want her to be more aware of how her words might affect others. On the other hand, she worked hard to get where she is. She studied, worked hard, and didn't settle for less. She deserves to be proud of her achievements and to talk about her job perks. It's natural to want to share positive things about your life. Maybe I'm being too sensitive or projecting my own insecurities onto her. I also need to consider how she feels. She might feel that I'm dismissing her hard work and achievements by telling her to be more modest. She might feel that I'm jealous, which could strain our relationship. It's important to communicate my feelings without making her feel bad about her successes. Perhaps I should approach the conversation differently. Instead of telling her to stop talking about her work perks, I could express how her comments make me feel. Maybe something like, "I feel uncomfortable when you talk about your job perks because I know not everyone has that, and I don't want others to feel bad or for us to be seen as flaunting our lifestyle." That way, it's about my feelings rather than criticizing her. I also need to reflect on whether my jealousy is justified. Am I feeling insecure about my own situation? If so, maybe I need to work on that separately rather than projecting it onto her. In the end, I think I might be being a bit AITA because I'm focusing on her behavior without considering her perspective and the effort she put into her job. However, it's also valid for me to feel uncomfortable with how her comments might be perceived by others. The key is to communicate my feelings respectfully and find a middle ground where she can share her successes without making others feel bad.
